figure.name: Adam Smith
figure.role: Moral philosopher and political economist of markets, specialization, exchange, and commercial society.
figure.hook: Smith = markets and self-interest, but not a cartoon defense of greed.
whyHere: Smith belongs here because he helps explain the market road before socialism becomes a mass political argument.
That matters because later socialist critics are arguing with an economy shaped by markets, specialization, wages, commerce, and private accumulation.
figure.cleanIdea: Markets can coordinate many separate choices through exchange and prices, but that does not make markets morally complete or politically automatic.

ideas.title: Market
ideas.plainDefinition: A market is a system where people exchange goods, labor, money, or services through prices, supply, demand, and choice.
ideas.context: In the Smith path, markets are coordination machines: they can organize many separate decisions without one central planner.
ideas.whyMatters: Smith matters because market language becomes one foundation for capitalism. Later socialist arguments ask what markets coordinate well, what they hide, and who carries the cost when market freedom becomes worker dependency.
ideas.carefulVersion: Markets can coordinate information and opportunity. They can also hide coercion, monopoly, exclusion, pollution, debt pressure, and unequal starting points. A truth-first page has to study both the coordination power and the ledger of harm.

ideas.title: Division of Labor
ideas.plainDefinition: Division of labor means breaking work into specialized tasks so production becomes faster, more skilled, or more efficient.
ideas.context: In the Smith path, specialization helps explain modern productivity and the rise of commercial society.
ideas.whyMatters: Division of labor is one bridge from Smith to the Industrial Revolution. It helps explain why production can explode, while also setting up later questions about repetitive work, dependence, skill, wages, and worker power.
